hints.junior: A missing alt attribute and alt="" both look like 'no text' in the code — but only one of them tells a screen reader to skip the image.
hints.mid: The decorative banner and the real chart failed in opposite directions: one announced noise, the other announced nothing at all.
hints.staff: Same visual output, opposite accessibility-tree result — nothing in a screenshot-based QA pass would ever catch this.

hints.junior: Click 'Run screen reader pass' in each mode and watch what actually gets announced for each image.
hints.mid: Broken: the banner announces its filename and the chart says nothing. Fixed: the banner goes silent and the chart's real content gets read.
hints.staff: The fixed log removes an announcement from one image and adds one to the other — this bug touches both images at once, not just the one that looked broken.

hints.junior: Three states: a real description (read aloud), alt="" (skipped on purpose), and no attribute at all (screen readers often fall back to the filename).
hints.mid: One question per image: does it convey information the surrounding text doesn't already say? Yes, write it. No, alt="".
hints.staff: alt="" is a deliberate accessibility-tree removal instruction, not an absence of information — a missing attribute leaves the accessible-name computation nothing to work from but the filename.

hints.junior: An icon-only button's alt text should describe the action ('Delete'), not the icon ('trash can').
hints.mid: A chart's alt text stays short; the full data goes in a caption, a table, or an aria-describedby target next to it.
hints.staff: Audit for a CMS or component default that sets alt="" for anything without manually-entered text — it's correct for decoration and silently wrong for everything else, and it's invisible in a visual QA pass.

sections.junior: Today's case is about alt text — specifically two images on the same page that were both wrong about their alt attribute, in exactly opposite directions.
sections.mid: alt="" and a missing alt attribute look interchangeable in review, but they tell a screen reader opposite things.
sections.staff: Two independent authoring paths — a CMS default and a component with no alt prop wired up — converge on the same screenshot and diverge completely in the accessibility tree.

sections.junior: There are three states for an image's alt attribute: a real description that gets read aloud, an empty alt that tells the screen reader to skip it on purpose, and a missing attribute entirely, which often makes the screen reader fall back to reading the filename.
sections.mid: Ask one question: does this image convey information the surrounding text doesn't already say? Yes, write real alt text. No, mark it alt="" on purpose. Never leave it off.
sections.staff: alt="" is a deliberate instruction to remove the image from the accessibility tree — a missing attribute leaves nothing to work from, so it falls back to reading the filename.

sections.junior: Try running the simulated screen reader pass in each mode and listen to what actually gets announced for each image.
sections.mid: The broken banner announces a raw filename while the real chart goes silent — the fix reverses both at once.
sections.staff: Missing alt and wrongly-decorative alt are the same root mistake pointed in opposite directions, which is why fixing one image here touches both.

sections.junior: An empty alt and a missing alt attribute are not the same thing. Ask whether the image conveys information the text around it doesn't already say — if yes, describe it, if no, mark it empty on purpose.
sections.mid: Audit for missing alt attributes and blanket CMS-default empty alt separately — they hide opposite problems and neither shows up in a visual review.
sections.staff: Neither failure shows up in a visual review, because both render nothing visible — audit the accessibility tree, not the screenshot.
